newsitem.title: INDIA: India has not deployed missiles, Gujral says.
newsitem.headline: India has not deployed missiles, Gujral says.

text.p: Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral on Wednesday said reports that India had deployed its Prithvi missiles on its border with Pakistan were false.

"We have not deployed Prithvi in any part of India and more so on our borders," Gujral told reporters after inducting the first batch of Russian-built Sukhoi-30 fighter aircraft into the Indian Air Force in this western Indian city.

India has tested the 250-km (150-mile) Prithvi missile, and a 150-km (90-mile) variant, and has vowed to press ahead with its missile programme despite opposition from the United States and other countries.
Gujral said it was no secret that India had acquired missile technology but added that it was not true that it had deployed missiles on its border with Pakistan.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence in 1947. The neighbours' top diplomats are expected to resume a tenuous peace dialogue later this month.
"We have successfully acquired missile technology but we have not deployed the missiles as misleadingly reported," Gujral said.
"I do hope this message will be taken in because we are keen to pursue peace in this region and we shall continue to do it," he added.
He said the geopolitical situation and security environment did not permit "any let up in our defence preparedness".
Gujral said India was keen to send a message that it had no designs on any country and was committed to peace.
On Monday, the Hindu newspaper said India had stored, but not deployed, medium-range ballistic missiles near its border with Pakistan.
The newspaper said the Prithvi missiles had been taken to Jullundur city in the northwestern state of Punjab but not deployed. It did not say where the missiles had been made.

Last week the Washington Post reported that India had moved fewer than a dozen Prithvi missiles, which can carry conventional but not nuclear warheads, to a prospective launch site near the Pakistani border.
The eight twin-seat SU-30s inducted on Wednesday are the first of 40 India agreed to buy last year from Russia at a cost of $1.5 billion to $2.0 billion.

The multi-role fighter aircraft can be employed in both air defence and strike roles. It can carry up to eight tonnes of armaments and has a combat range of 3,000 km (1,880 miles) which can increase to 5,200 km (3,250 miles) with inflight refuelling.
After the induction ceremony Gujral, Defence Minister Mulayam Singh Yadav and Air Chief Marshal S.K. Sareen watched an aerobatics display by the Sukhoi 30s.
Three blue-coloured Sukhois, supported by four Jaguars and four MiG-29s, performed a series of low-level loops, rolls and knife-edge formations during the 30-minute show.
Gujral said the introduction of the Sukhois would make India's air force a power to reckon with over the next few decades.
He noted that the Sukhois were the first sophisticated fighter aircraft bought by India in about a decade.

India currently has 799 combat aircraft, including British-designed Jaguars, French Mirage 2000s and Russian MiGs, including the 21, 23, 27 and 29, according to the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies.
